title: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles — relationship

content.overview: Part III confers enforceable fundamental rights. Part IV states Directive Principles that are not enforceable by courts under Article 37, yet fundamental in governance. Indian constitutional law developed toward harmonisation of the two Parts, constrained by the basic structure doctrine and by the limited surviving operation of Article 31C. Verify current scope of Article 31C against the official text and controlling Supreme Court authority before advising on any statute.

sections.heading: Textual starting point
sections.body: Article 37: Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court. Fundamental Rights under Part III are enforceable (Articles 32 and 226). Any relationship analysis begins with that asymmetry.

sections.heading: Historical conflict and harmonisation
sections.body: Early decisions sometimes treated Directive Principles as subordinate when they conflicted with Fundamental Rights. Later jurisprudence emphasised reading the Constitution as a whole so that, as far as possible, Part III and Part IV support each other. Harmonious construction is a method of interpretation, not a licence to ignore Article 37 or to invent a freestanding Part IV cause of action.

sections.heading: Article 31C (careful)
sections.body: Article 31C saves certain laws giving effect to specified Directive Principles from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, within the limits of the surviving constitutional text. The Twenty-fifth Amendment introduced Article 31C; later amendment history and Supreme Court decisions (including Minerva Mills) are essential to the present scope. Do not assert an expanded or narrowed reading of Article 31C without checking the official text and the ratio of the controlling cases. Citation of case names here is orientation only — verify the report before courtroom use.

sections.heading: Basic structure
sections.body: The basic structure doctrine limits constitutional amendments that would destroy essential features of the Constitution. Interaction between Directive Principles, Fundamental Rights, and amending power must be argued from Kesavananda, Minerva Mills and later authorities as actually decided — without inventing holdings.

sections.heading: Present practice
sections.body: CURRENT POSITION (practice-oriented): (1) No direct enforcement of a Directive Principle as a right under Article 32 solely because it appears in Part IV. (2) Implementing legislation and executive schemes are the primary vehicles. (3) Part III challenges remain available against State action; Directive Principles may inform reasonableness and purpose analysis where judicial doctrine allows. (4) Article 31C questions require text-and-authority verification for the specific statute and year.
